name: sample_rag_wikipedia
description: Small sample (10 cases) to check the pipeline end to end. Write your own 30-50 cases for a real experiment.

cases.question: In what year was retrieval-augmented generation first proposed?
What incorrect information did Google's Bard give in its first demonstration, and what did it cost Google?
cases.expected_answer: Bard gave incorrect information about the James Webb Space Telescope, contributing to a $100 billion decline in Google's stock value.

cases.question: What is the technique of adding relevant context to the user's input called?
Where are the embeddings stored so that documents can be retrieved?
How do sparse vectors differ from dense vectors?
cases.expected_answer: Sparse vectors encode the identity of a word, are dictionary-length and mostly zeros; dense vectors encode meaning, are more compact and contain fewer zeros.
evidence: Sparse vectors, which encode the identity of a word

cases.question: What task can be used to pre-train the retriever?
cases.expected_answer: The Inverse Cloze Task (ICT), which has the model predict masked text within documents.

cases.question: What is the more reproducible version of Retro called?
What trade-off does chunk size involve?
cases.expected_answer: A trade-off between focused retrieval and contextual completeness: smaller chunks isolate relevant information but can omit context, while larger chunks keep context but may include irrelevant material and use more of the input budget.
evidence: trade-off between focused retrieval and contextual completeness

cases.question: How does hybrid search help when vector search misses key facts?
cases.expected_answer: It also runs a traditional full-text search and combines those results with the vector-search chunks before feeding them to the language model.

cases.question: Does RAG prevent hallucinations?
cases.expected_answer: No. RAG does not prevent hallucinations; the model can still hallucinate around the source material.
